nodes.label: ADR 0007: the shared secret becomes an enrollment token, per-era keys wrapped per peer
nodes.rationale: Status proposed, not implemented. One 32-byte secret is the whole security model today: possession of the secret is membership, no PKI and no per-peer identity. Adding a machine hands over the key that decrypts everyone's traffic forever including the past; removing a machine forces every remaining peer to take a new secret; and there is no way to grant read-from-now-on without granting read-everything. The third blocks adoption.

nodes.label: The 32-byte shared workspace secret
nodes.rationale: protocol/crypto.ts:5 states that possession of the secret is membership. It survives rather than being replaced because the alternative hands membership to the transport: today GitHub cannot read a workspace's traffic under any circumstances because the secret never goes near it, and that property is the difference between dead-drop and a shared private repository.

nodes.label: deriveWorkspaceKey (crypto.ts:68)
nodes.rationale: HKDFs the shared secret straight into the AES-256-GCM key every frame is sealed under. Deterministic, which is what makes a 0.12.0 workspace's key id computable by a new build and gives migration a clean shape.

nodes.label: The secret as an enrollment token
nodes.rationale: The secret stops being a data key and becomes a proof key. Whoever holds it can enroll at any moment with no existing peer online and no approval step, which is the user's stated constraint (2026-08-11: anyone may join at any time, no owner approves, onboarding stays very easy). Whoever controls the transport but not the secret cannot forge a proof, which is what the threat model requires since crypto.ts:7 treats the store as hostile. Costs nothing at the surface: ddrop init --github <owner>/<repo> --secret - is unchanged.

nodes.label: Per-peer X25519 identity
nodes.rationale: Each peer generates a keypair on first start and keeps the private half in .deaddrop/identity, mode 0600, beside the secret. X25519 because the wrap is a Diffie-Hellman and Ed25519 cannot do DH; Node v26.7.0 provides both natively so no dependency is added, keeping invariant 6 satisfied without argument. Losing .deaddrop/identity is a real loss: recovery is re-enrolling under a new identity with the secret, a backup consideration that did not exist before.

nodes.label: Enrollment proof (HMAC over workspace, peerId, publicKey)
nodes.rationale: proofKey = HKDF(secret, info = 'dead-drop/v1/enrollment'); proof = HMAC-SHA256(proofKey, workspace || peerId || publicKey). A peer accepts an identity only if the proof verifies.

nodes.label: ws/<workspace>/ids/<peer>.ddi identity objects
nodes.rationale: Where a peer publishes its public key plus proof.

nodes.label: Era key
nodes.rationale: 32 random bytes whose id is the existing scheme, the first 8 hex chars of SHA-256 over the derived key. Frames do not change at all: keyId already means 'which key sealed this'. Several live eras at once is not a special case, it is what KeyRing was written for.

nodes.label: Wrapped era key at keys/<peer>/<eraId>.ddw
nodes.rationale: The era key is sealed to each recipient's public key by X25519 ECDH into HKDF into AES-256-GCM. Grouped by peer, not by era: the record originally said keys/<eraId>/<peer>.ddw and implementation exposed that as wrong, because a peer has to find every key addressed to it, so grouping by era forces a sweep of every era ever on every cycle while grouping by peer is a single prefix listing with the same shape as inbox/<peer>/.

nodes.label: KeyRing (crypto.ts:116)
nodes.rationale: Already holds an active key plus every key still accepted during a rotation, and crypto.ts:144 reports an unknown key id with the list it does know. Its asymmetry is exactly what wrapping needs: sealing always uses the primary, opening tries whichever key id the frame names (crypto.ts:117), so a peer seals under one era of its own and reads any era it has been given.

nodes.label: Frame keyId header field
nodes.rationale: frame.ts:8-9 puts keyIdLen and keyId in the clear header, outside the ciphertext and inside the AAD (frame.ts:95). crypto.ts:12 already declares that a departing peer triggers a rotation and that the key id is what makes an overlap possible, so the protocol was built expecting more than one key in play; nothing has ever put a second one there.

nodes.label: Why frames are left alone
nodes.rationale: Carrying wrapped keys inside each message is worse on three checkable counts: every frame grows by one wrapped key per recipient; the recipient count becomes visible on every object, a new class of metadata leak rather than an extension of the documented one; and a broadcast to a topic has no recipient list at write time because subscribers are discovered by polling. Separate key objects keep the frame format byte-identical, move the metadata cost into a key layout that already leaks peer names by design, and let a topic frame be sealed once per era rather than once per subscriber.

nodes.label: Joining and removing a peer
nodes.rationale: A joiner publishes its identity with a proof, mints its own era key, wraps it for every identity it can verify, and can send immediately. It becomes readable-to itself once any existing peer notices the identity and publishes a wrapped copy of that peer's era, on an ordinary poll with no human involved. Removal: mint a new era, wrap it for everyone except the leaver, stop sealing under the old one. Nobody redistributes a secret and nobody else re-keys; the leaver keeps whatever it already had, which is unavoidable in every scheme.

nodes.label: Opt-in strict tier: enrollment.requireApproval
nodes.rationale: Withholds wrapping from a newly seen identity until a human runs ddrop peer approve <peer> <fingerprint> with a fingerprint compared outside the transport. Off by default. The knob for operators who do not trust their transport at the moment of enrollment, and the only part that costs a step.

nodes.label: Encryption never becomes optional
nodes.rationale: Not as a flag, not as a default, not as a 'just for testing' path. A user who believes traffic is protected and is wrong is worse off than one who knows it is not, and the frame format already supports keyIdLen = 0 for unencrypted frames, a foot-gun that should not gain a config surface pointing at it.

nodes.label: Rejected: trust on first use, no secret at all
nodes.rationale: Simplest possible onboarding and it dissolves the threat model: if a peer enrolls by publishing a public key with no proof, whoever can write to the store can enroll themselves, and for a private GitHub repository that is GitHub. Rejected because it removes the reason the project encrypts anything, in exchange for removing a flag the join command already fills in from stdin.

nodes.label: Rejected: mandatory out-of-band fingerprint approval
nodes.rationale: Strongest option and the only one that survives a transport compromised at the moment of enrollment. It adds a manual step to every new machine, against the stated direction that usability must not mean long steps, so it ships as requireApproval instead of as the default.

nodes.label: Rejected: per-pair keys with no shared era key
nodes.rationale: Removes the era concept and with it any efficient broadcast: a topic message would have to be sealed once per subscriber, by a writer that does not know who the subscribers are.

nodes.label: Rejected: optional encryption or a plaintext mode
nodes.rationale: Rejected outright, on the grounds that a false belief in protection is worse than a known absence of it.

nodes.label: Migration from the secret-derived key
nodes.rationale: The secret-derived key is deterministic, so a 0.12.0 workspace's key id is computable by a new build. New peers keep deriving it, keep accepting it as an era, and publish an identity alongside it, so a partially upgraded workspace keeps working in both directions; the old era stops being used only on an explicit operator rotate. Without this, upgrading one machine silently partitions the workspace, the failure mode most worth a scenario test. Along with the reaper interaction it is one of the two places most likely to be wrong, and both deserve mutation-verified tests on ADR 0006's standard.

nodes.label: The enrolled-but-deaf state
nodes.rationale: An identity published with nobody yet having wrapped an era for it decodes nothing and looks exactly like a wrong secret. ddrop peers and ddrop status must name that state or the first support question is unanswerable; crypto.ts:144 already reports the key ids it holds, which is the right raw material.

nodes.label: Reapers must be taught two new prefixes
nodes.rationale: Identity objects and wrapped era keys are long-lived by nature and belong to peers that may be offline for weeks. Under ADR 0006's age-plus-absence judgement they would be collected and the workspace would quietly lose the ability to admit or address that peer. They must be excluded explicitly, with a test asserting the exclusion rather than the code merely happening to skip them.

nodes.label: Metadata cost of ids/ and keys/
nodes.rationale: They expose peer names and a peer count to anyone who can read the store. Peer names are already exposed by peers/<peer>.ddf and inbox/<peer>/, which invariant 9 covers explicitly. The genuinely new fact is the count of peers per era, a coarse membership-size signal: small, stated here rather than discovered later, and it does not touch frame contents, so invariant 9 holds as written.

nodes.label: Invariant 6 (no new dependencies)
nodes.rationale: Satisfied without argument because Node v26.7.0 provides X25519 and Ed25519 natively.

hyperedges.label: Per-era key distribution: enroll, wrap, unwrap, seal
